title: Recording: Tragedy by Wings | 1972
content:
Studio One, Olympic Studios, London
Producer: Glyn Johns
Engineer: Phil Chapman

Wings recorded a cover version of Thomas Wayne Perkins’ 1959 hit ‘Tragedy’ on 13 March 1972.

The song was written by Gerald H Nelson and Fred B Burch, and first recorded in 1958 by Thomas Wayne and the DeLons. Released the following year, it peaked at number five on the US Billboard Hot 100, becoming Wayne’s only hit single.

The song had a resurgence following Perkins’ death in a car accident in August 1971, and Paul and Linda McCartney became fans.

Wings’ version featured Paul on bass guitar, Denny Laine and Henry McCullough on acoustic guitars, and Denny Seiwell on drums. They recorded eight takes, the last of which became the master. The overdubs included lead and harmony vocals.

Wings’ second album Red Rose Speedway was originally conceived as a double album. A two-disc acetate version of the album, dated 13 December 1972, had ‘Tragedy’ kicking off side two.

During research for the 2018 reissue of the album, MPL uncovered what they claimed was the final tracklisting for the double album. Red Rose Speedway: Reconstructed was released in December 2018 as a bonus CD in the deluxe edition of the album, and separately as a two-LP vinyl version.

During the research, either the essay writer or MPL aim to speak with as many of the musicians, producers and engineers from the period as we can – we always want the story to be as complete as possible. So we jumped out of our seats when we learned that Denny Seiwell (drummer on Wild Life and Red Rose Speedway) still had three of the four acetates of a version of the touted release. And luckily the tracklisting for the fourth side was also written on there – so we had a physical document from the time! (You can see scans of these acetates in the 128-page essay book included in the Deluxe Edition.)
paulmccartney.com, 26 December 2018

The final double album had ‘Tragedy’ as the penultimate song on side three, followed by ‘Little Lamb Dragonfly’.
